User Guide: Running a Cost-Effectiveness Analysis in the App

This guide is for someone opening ShinyCEA for the first time. It explains what the app does, then walks through a complete analysis of the bundled Sick-Sicker model, from launching the app in R to exporting the code.

What the App Does

ShinyCEA is an R package with a point-and-click app for cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA): comparing the costs and health effects (QALYs) of several strategies to decide which one gives the best value. You give it a decision model; the app runs the analyses and draws the tables and figures.

Analysis Tab Question it answers
Base case Deterministic Which strategy is best at the expected parameter values? Which are dominated?
One- and two-way sensitivity Deterministic Which parameters move the result most?
Threshold Threshold At what value of a parameter does the decision change?
Probabilistic (PSA) PSA, PSA Parameters How uncertain are costs and QALYs when all parameters vary together?
Acceptability and expected loss CEAC How likely is each strategy to be cost-effective, and how much is lost by choosing wrongly?
Value of information VOI What is it worth to reduce uncertainty, and for which parameters?
Model behaviour Survival, Traces How does the cohort move through the health states?
Scenarios and subgroups Scenarios, Subgroups Do results hold under other assumptions or patient groups?
Weighted comparators Weighted How do mixes of strategies (e.g. market shares) compare?
Budget impact BIA What does adopting a strategy cost the payer over the next years?
Equity Equity How are health gains distributed across groups?
Checks Health, Validation Are the parameters and model outputs sound?

The Example: Sick-Sicker

The Sick-Sicker model is a 4-state Markov cohort model. People start Healthy, can become Sick, then Sicker, and can die from any state. It compares standard care (std) with four treatments (t1 to t4) that differ in their effect on progression and mortality and in their drug cost, over 10 years in 3-month cycles.

Step 1: Launch the App from R

Install the package once, then load it and start the app with the model:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("CarlosPiant/ShinyCEA")

library(ShinyCEA)
run_cea_app(cea_sick_sicker())

run_cea_app() with no arguments opens all bundled example models with a model selector; pass your own model to analyse it instead (see vignette("custom-models")).

The app opens in your browser on the Model Info tab:

The sidebar on the left holds the settings shared by all analyses:

  • Data: upload a CSV of parameter values (optional).
  • Reference: the comparator for incremental results. Auto picks the strategy with the highest net monetary benefit; Pinned lets you choose.
  • WTP: willingness to pay per QALY.
  • PSA iterations and PSA seed: size of the probabilistic analysis and the random seed that makes it repeatable.
  • R code for this tab and Reports: export the code or a Word/PDF report.
  • Run Deterministic and Run PSA (bottom): the two buttons that run the model. Most tabs stay empty until you click them.

Step 2: Review the Parameters

Open Parameters to see every input of the model. base is the value used in the base case, lower and upper are the range for sensitivity analyses, and distribution is what the PSA samples from. Double-click a cell to edit it; include_psa and include_tornado switch a parameter in or out of those analyses.

The Health tab checks the table for problems (for example a probability above 1) and should show no FAIL before you continue.

Step 3: Run the Base Case

Click Run Deterministic, then open Deterministic. The results table lists each strategy’s cost, QALYs and net monetary benefit (NMB), with the increments and ICER against the reference. Here t4 has the highest NMB at a WTP of 100,000, so it is the reference and the preferred strategy.

Further down the same tab:

  • the frontier table and plot, which flag dominated and extendedly dominated strategies;
  • the tornado diagram, which ranks parameters by how much they move the result for the target strategy you choose;
  • the two-way sensitivity analysis, a heat map over two parameters.

The Threshold tab searches for the value of one parameter at which the ICER reaches the WTP: choose the strategy, the parameter and the range, then click Run threshold search. Survival and Traces show the base-case survival curves and the share of the cohort in each state over time:

Step 4: Run the Probabilistic Analysis

Set PSA iterations (1,000 or more for final results) and click Run PSA. The PSA tab shows the cost-effectiveness plane, one point per iteration and strategy relative to the reference, and a summary with 95% intervals. PSA Parameters shows the distributions that were sampled.

Open CEAC for the acceptability curves: the probability that each strategy is cost-effective at each WTP. Tick Superimpose the acceptability frontier (CEAF) to mark the strategy with the highest expected net benefit.

Below it, the expected loss curves show how much net benefit is forgone, on average, by choosing each strategy. The lowest curve is the optimal strategy, and its height is the EVPI.

The VOI tab plots the EVPI across WTP values and the EVPPI, which ranks parameters by the value of resolving their uncertainty:

See vignette("acceptability-expected-loss") and vignette("value-of-information") for how to read these figures.

Step 5: Scenarios, Subgroups and Budget Impact

These tabs each have their own run button and do not need the PSA.

Scenarios. A scenario changes one or more parameter values. The Sick-Sicker model comes with six (for example No discounting); add your own with a name, a parameter and a new value. Click Run all scenarios to compare results and see the optimal strategy in each.

Subgroups. Works the same way for patient groups: choose a target and a reference strategy, click Run subgroup analysis, and read the forest plot.

BIA. Enter the target population, the projection years, and the market shares today and in the final year, then click Run BIA for the yearly and total budget impact.

Weighted compares mixes of strategies, Equity shows how health gains are distributed across the model’s subgroups, and Validation runs a set of automated checks and gives the model a score. Each works with one click on its run button.

Step 6: Export the Code and a Report

Click R code for this tab on any tab to see the R script that reproduces it with the values you selected. Choose Full script (all tabs) for the whole analysis, then copy it or download it as an .R file. Because the script uses the PSA seed from the sidebar, its results match the app.

The exported script uses the same functions you can call yourself. The core of the Sick-Sicker analysis is:

library(ShinyCEA)

model  <- cea_sick_sicker()
params <- sanitize_params(model$default_params())$df
wtp    <- 100000

# Base case
det <- run_deterministic(model, params, wtp = wtp)
det$table

# Probabilistic analysis, CEAC and expected loss
set.seed(20250605)
psa  <- run_psa(model, params, n_sim = 1000)
ceac <- compute_ceac(psa$results, det$strategies)
plot_ceac(ceac, ceaf = compute_ceaf(psa$results, det$strategies))
plot_expected_loss(compute_expected_loss(psa$results, det$strategies), show_optimal = TRUE)

The Word and PDF buttons under Reports build a document with the tables and figures of the analyses you have run. Every table and plot also has its own download button, and Settings changes the colour palette of all figures.

A Typical Session

  1. run_cea_app(cea_sick_sicker())
  2. Check Parameters and Health; set WTP and the reference.
  3. Run Deterministic: read the results, frontier and tornado.
  4. Run PSA: read the CE plane, CEAC, expected loss and VOI.
  5. Run Scenarios, Subgroups and BIA as needed.
  6. Export the R code and a report.

If you change a parameter, the WTP, the reference or the seed after a run, the app shows a banner saying the results are out of date: click the run buttons again to refresh them.
